title: Loved by Allah and by people
word: Loved by Allah and by people
hook: renounce the world and Allah loves you, renounce what people have and they love you
tomorrow: someone hurts you first. are you allowed to hurt them back?

segments.voice: Yesterday, what He left unsaid: duties kept firm, and open space left on purpose. Silence is mercy too. Today, the advice that sounded backward.
screen: `SILENCE IS MERCY TOO.` → `ADVICE THAT SOUNDS BACKWARD.`

segments.voice: A friend who never asks for anything is strangely easy to love. The one who always needs a ride, a charger, a favor, gets loved too, just more tiredly. So, yesterday's question. A man comes to the Prophet, peace be upon him, and asks for a deed that will make Allah love him and people love him. The answer, in paraphrase from Ibn Majah's collection: renounce the world, and Allah will love you. Renounce what people have, and people will love you.
screen: `THE FRIEND WHO NEVER ASKS.` → `ONE DEED, TWO LOVES.` → `RENOUNCE, AND BE LOVED.`

segments.voice: The word under it is zuhd: wanting little, letting go. The second half is plain enough: stop eyeing what other people have, and they relax around you. The first half is where two views live inside the tradition. One view: zuhd means really letting go, in the hands. Own little, eat simply, keep the world at arm's length. Tradition tells of people who walked away from wealth for this. Their best case: what you hold ends up holding you. Full hands can't reach for anything else. The other view: zuhd lives in the heart, not the hands. Ibn Rajab, writing on this very hadith, reports that Imam Ahmad was asked whether someone with a lot of money could still have zuhd. He said yes, if he doesn't rejoice when it grows or grieve when it shrinks. Their best case: empty hands can hide a very busy heart, and wealth can be held loosely and given away. Both views agree on more than they fight about. The world isn't the enemy; the grip is. And here's the line to tell a friend tonight: in this hadith, being loved by people comes from what you don't want from them.
screen: `ZUHD: WANTING LITTLE.` · `VIEW ONE: LET GO IN THE HANDS.` · `VIEW TWO: LET GO IN THE HEART.` · `THE GRIP, NOT THE WORLD.` · then, large: `WANT LESS, BE LOVED.`

segments.voice: Count on your fingers what you already have today that you didn't need to ask anyone for: this breath, a hand that works, water nearby, a place to sit. With each finger, notice the small ease of not needing one more thing. When you run out of fingers, start the count again.
screen: `COUNT WHAT YOU ALREADY HAVE.` · `NOTHING TO ASK FOR.`

segments.voice: Loved by Allah and by people: the two loves in hadith thirty-one, one from letting go of the world, one from letting go of what others have.
screen: `LOVED BY ALLAH AND BY PEOPLE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Keep this one: want less, be loved, and loosen the grip on what's yours and what's theirs. That's hadith thirty-one.

howItsDone: Muslim teachers explain zuhd in different ways: some stress simple living and owning little, others stress a heart that holds wealth loosely; both warn against coveting what others have.

pairs: no joy at gain, no grief at loss

myth: zuhd means owning nothing; anyone with money can't have it
that's one view. Imam Ahmad said someone with wealth can, if the heart doesn't cling to it.
in this hadith, people's love comes from not wanting what they have
renounce what people have, and people will love you.

fork.setup: your cousin says zuhd means owning almost nothing. you lean toward 'it's in the heart.' to be fair, what's her best case?

fork.reveal: the hands-first view's real argument: full hands can't reach for anything else. the heart-first view answers that empty hands can hide a busy heart. both live inside the tradition.

original.note: Arabic: renounce the world, and Allah will love you. izhad comes from the same root as zuhd.

trapdoor: what you thought: be a minimalist and people will like you.
what it means: let go of the world and Allah loves you; stop coveting what others have and people do.
what a scholar hears: Ibn Majah's report; Ibn Rajab's commentary and Imam Ahmad's answer that zuhd is about the heart's grip.
guess: loved for letting go, by Allah and by others
admired for praying more than other people
liked for giving people all that they ask

chat.says: i'm supposed to ask shops to donate for Leo's family. doesn't 'renounce what people have' mean don't ask?
options: It's about wanting their stuff for yourself. Asking for Leo, wanting nothing back, is different.
Yes. Asking anyone for anything breaks the hadith, even when it's for somebody else.
Ask for anything you like. Zuhd is just a private feeling, so asking never matters.
chat.meaning: The hadith warns against coveting what people have. Asking on someone else's behalf, with nothing in it for you, isn't that.

zuhd.meaning: wanting little; letting go of the world's grip

Ibn Majah.meaning: a scholar whose hadith collection records this report

Ibn Rajab.meaning: a scholar who wrote a famous commentary on the forty

Imam Ahmad.meaning: Ahmad ibn Hanbal, a great early scholar of hadith and law
